title: SwiftUI performance
summary: Keep `body` cheap and make each view depend on as little data as possible. Measure with the SwiftUI instrument, fix the worst view, measure again.
body: **In simple words:** SwiftUI is fast when `body` is light and few views refresh per change. It gets slow when a big view depends on fast-changing data or when `body` does heavy work.
**Workflow:** reproduce the slow screen → profile with Instruments (SwiftUI template: body updates and why they happened; Hitches; Time Profiler) → fix the top offender → measure again.

**Main rules:** (1) No heavy work in `body` (no sorting, date formatting of big lists, I/O) - precompute in the model. (2) Split big views into small ones so a change refreshes only a small part. (3) Pass only the data a child needs, not the whole model. (4) Use `List`/`LazyVStack` for long lists with stable ids. (5) Avoid `AnyView` and per-row `GeometryReader`.
**Images:** downsample big images to display size off the main thread and cache them. `AsyncImage` has no disk cache, so feeds usually need a custom loader.
**Debug trick:** `let _ = Self._printChanges()` inside `body` prints why it re-ran.
keyPoints: Measure first (SwiftUI instrument, Time Profiler, Hitches).
Lazy containers with stable ids for long lists.
Downsample and cache images off main.
`Self._printChanges()` to see what triggered a body update.

code.caption: Narrow dependencies

mistakes: Storing scroll offset or timer values in the environment or a root model, redrawing everything.
followups: **Why might a list scroll badly?** Heavy rows, full-size image decoding on main, unstable ids, GeometryReader per row.
**What does `.drawingGroup()` do?** Renders complex vector content into one Metal-backed image.
